A Bloomberg report suggests that Apple Glasses may launch without photo or video recording capabilities. Apple is reportedly considering this approach to alleviate privacy concerns.

That said, while I fully understand why the company would have such concerns, based on my personal experience using Ray-Ban Meta glasses, video recording is absolutely the most essential feature of this type of product…

Privacy is a major consideration in many of Apple's decisions and one of the selling points of its ecosystem.

For example, when it comes to AI features, Apple is committed to processing everything on-device wherever possible. When cloud computing is necessary, its Private Cloud Compute design aims to ensure Apple cannot access user data and allows security researchers to verify this independently. This is undoubtedly a good thing.

The Privacy Controversy of Smart Glasses

Undeniably, smart glasses equipped with video recording do raise privacy concerns. This was one of the main reasons for Google Glass's failure, with users even being given the embarrassing nickname "Glassholes".

Ray-Ban Meta glasses have also sparked privacy controversies, partly because some YouTubers used the product in extremely unethical ways, as reported earlier this year by BBC News.

The company also faced criticism for being caught sending sensitive video clips, including accidentally recorded footage, to human data annotators.

For all these reasons, I completely understand why Apple would have reservations about adding video recording capability to Apple Glasses.

But Video Recording Is a Critical Feature

The challenge Apple faces is that video recording is a core feature of today's smart glasses. Based on my personal experience, if a product cannot record video, I wouldn't even consider wearing it.

Let me first list the various features of the Ray-Ban Meta, then share my actual experience with each one:

  • Ask Meta AI about what you're looking at
  • Play music
  • Hands-free voice calls, including making and answering
  • Receive voice notifications, including reading out received messages
  • Capture first-person photos via button or voice command
  • Capture first-person video via button or voice command

Ask the AI questions

Meta positions this as one of the main reasons to buy the glasses, and it does make a strong first impression. For example, you can look at a famous landmark and have the glasses provide relevant information. It can also identify various objects, from flowers to sculptures. The experience is like having Apple Intelligence with you everywhere, without needing to pull your phone from your pocket.

I tested these features extensively when I first bought them and was excited about the future possibilities. I imagined being able to walk past different restaurants and have the glasses instantly tell me each one's average TripAdvisor rating and dishes past customers had recommended.

However, in the current state of affairs, I have almost never used this feature and would certainly not consider it sufficient reason for me to wear smart glasses daily.

Playing Music

Not recommended: the tiny speakers built into the temples never deliver ideal sound quality. Headphones are always a better choice, and in-ear headphones are just as convenient.

Hands-free Voice Calls

Being able to briefly take calls while cycling can occasionally be practical, since I don't want to wear in-ear headphones that block ambient sound. But as soon as a conversation goes beyond a few sentences, I'll stop and get off the bike, so this feature also isn't enough reason for me to wear smart glasses daily.

Voice Notifications

I do like this feature. Whether it's iMessage or WhatsApp messages, I can have the glasses read them out while I continue walking or cycling. But again, this benefit alone isn't enough to make me buy the product.

Photo and Video Recording

This is the biggest selling point of today's smart glasses. Being able to capture first-person footage without using a phone is incredibly convenient, whether it's for special experiences like roller coasters or sailing, or for revisiting holiday or weekend trips. As I mentioned in my earlier review of the Ray-Ban Meta glasses:

I also found it a great way to document my cycling rides. Since I already wear sunglasses, all I need to do is press a button on the temple, saving me the hassle of mounting an action camera on the bike. Motorcycle enthusiasts use it the same way.

This feature is the biggest reason I wear smart glasses, and if I lost this benefit, I honestly wouldn't use them at all. For me, Apple Glasses without photo and video recording capabilities hold zero appeal. (Smart glasses with displays are a different matter—I will share my experience with them in another article, but that's not what we expect from the first generation of Apple Glasses.)

What Should Apple Do?

The good news is I don't think it's impossible to strike a balance between practicality and privacy.

One of the commonly criticised aspects of the Ray-Ban Meta glasses is that while it has a flashing LED light to indicate it's recording, the visibility of this indicator is not great in bright sunlight. Apple could easily ensure its LED indicator is designed for high visibility.

Apple could also install speakers on the outside of the temples that emit sound effects when recording starts and stops, letting people nearby know. Another approach would be to eliminate the physical button for photo and video entirely, requiring users to issue voice commands instead. Both methods would make it clear to those around the user that they are being filmed.

Of course, there's no perfect solution. One cannot prevent someone from starting to record from a distance and then approaching their subject. But I think combining these privacy-preserving features would work in the vast majority of situations.

What Apple needs to achieve isn't perfection, but making misuse significantly more difficult, so that those with ill intent wouldn't choose this device for wrongdoing.

What are your thoughts on this dilemma? Feel free to share your opinions in the comments section.
